entries.563322877209781673ebfb3809b373b50c4eb60d: <div sID="gen1862" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="21" osisID="Exod.21" sID="Exod.21"/> <div eID="gen1862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1863" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen1864" type="x-p"/> The laws recorded in this chapter relate to the fifth and sixth commandments; and though they are not accommodated to our constitution, especially in point of servitude, nor are the penalties annexed binding on us, yet they are of great use for the explanation of the moral law, and the rules of natural justice. Here are several enlargements, I. Upon the fifth commandment, which concerns particular relations. 1. The duty of masters towards their servants, their men-servants (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.2-Exod.21.6">ver. 2-6</reference>), and the maidservants, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.7-Exod.21.11">ver. 7-11</reference>. 2. The punishment of disobedient children that strike their parents (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.15">ver. 15</reference>), or curse them, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.17">ver. 17</reference>. II. Upon the sixth commandment, which forbids all violence offered to the person of a man. Here is, 1. Concerning murder, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.12-Exod.21.14">ver. 12-14</reference>. 2. Man-stealing, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.16">ver. 16</reference>. 3. Assault and battery, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.18-Exod.21.19">ver. 18, 19</reference>. 4. Correcting a servant, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.20-Exod.21.21">ver. 20, 21</reference>. 5. Hurting a woman with child, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.22-Exod.21.23">ver. 22, 23</reference>. 6. The law of retaliation, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.24-Exod.21.25">ver. 24, 25</reference>. 7. Maiming a servant, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.26">ver. 26, 27</reference>. 8. An ox goring, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.28-Exod.21.32">ver. 28-32</reference>. 9. Damage by opening a pit, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.33-Exod.21.34">ver. 33, 34</reference>. 10. Cattle fighting, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.35-Exod.21.36">ver. 35, 36</reference>.
entries.79f4fb6e20944c85beb5709bf0f2e8519ea8c0af: <div eID="gen1864" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen1863" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Judicial Laws. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1491.)</title> <div sID="gen1865" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the judgments which thou shalt set before them. <hi type="super">2</hi> If thou buy an Hebrew servant, six years he shall serve: and in the seventh he shall go out free for nothing. <hi type="super">3</hi> If he came in by himself, he shall go out by himself: if he were married, then his wife shall go out with him. 4 If his master have given him a wife, and she have born him sons or daughters; the wife and her children shall be her master's, and he shall go out by himself. <hi type="super">5</hi> And if the servant shall plainly say, I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free: <hi type="super">6</hi> Then his master shall bring him unto the judges; he shall also bring him to the door, or unto the door post; and his master shall bore his ear through with an awl; and he shall serve him for ever. <hi type="super">7</hi> And if a man sell his daughter to be a maidservant, she shall not go out as the menservants do. <hi type="super">8</hi> If she please not her master, who hath betrothed her to himself, then shall he let her be redeemed: to sell her unto a strange nation he shall have no power, seeing he hath dealt deceitfully with her. <hi type="super">9</hi> And if he have betrothed her unto his son, he shall deal with her after the manner of daughters. <hi type="super">10</hi> If he take him another <hi type="italic">wife;</hi> her food, her raiment, and her duty of marriage, shall he not diminish. <hi type="super">11</hi> And if he do not these three unto her, then shall she go out free without money. <div eID="gen1865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1866" type="x-p"/> The <reference osisRef="Exod.21.1">first verse</reference> is the general title of the laws contained in this and the two following chapters, some of them relating to the religious worship of God, but most of them relating to matters between man and man. Their government being purely a Theocracy, that which in other states is to be settled by human prudence was directed among them by a divine appointment, so that the constitution of their government was peculiarly adapted to make them happy. These laws are called <hi type="italic">judgments,</hi> because they are framed in infinite wisdom and equity, and because their magistrates were to give judgment according to the people. In the doubtful cases that had hitherto occurred, Moses had particularly enquired of God for them, as appeared, <reference osisRef="Exod.18.15">ch. xviii. 15</reference>; but now God gave him statutes in general by which to determine particular cases, which likewise he must apply to other like cases that might happen, which, falling under the same reason, fell under the same rule. He begins with the laws concerning servants, commanding mercy and moderation towards them. The Israelites had lately been servants themselves; and now that they had become, not only their own masters, but masters of servants, too, lest they should abuse their servants, as they themselves had been abused and ruled with rigour by the Egyptian task-masters, provision was made by these laws for the mild and gentle usage of servants. Note, If those who have had power over us have been injurious to us this will not in the least excuse us if we be in like manner injurious to those who are under our power, but will rather aggravate our crime, because, in that case, we may the more easily put our souls into their soul's stead. Here is, <div eID="gen1866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1867" type="x-p"/> I. A law concerning men-servants, sold, either by themselves or their parents, through poverty, or by the judges, for their crimes; even those of the latter sort (if Hebrews) were to continue in slavery but seven years at the most, in which time it was taken for granted that they would sufficiently have smarted for their folly or offence. At the seven years' end the servant should either go out free (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.2-Exod.21.3">v. 2, 3</reference>), or his servitude should thenceforward be his choice, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.5-Exod.21.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. If he had a wife given him by his master, and children, he might either leave them and go out free himself, or, if he had such a kindness for them that he would rather tarry with them in bondage than go out at liberty without them, he was to have his ear bored through to the doorpost and serve till the death of his master, or the year of jubilee. <div eID="gen1867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1868" type="x-p"/> 1. By this law God taught, (1.) The Hebrew servants generosity, and a noble love of liberty, for they were the Lord's freemen; a mark of disgrace must be put upon him who refused liberty when he might have it, though he refused it upon considerations otherwise laudable enough. Thus Christians, being <hi type="italic">bought with a price, and called unto liberty,</hi> must not be the servants of men, nor of the lusts of men, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.23">1 Cor. vii. 23</reference>. There is a free and princely spirit that much helps to uphold a Christian, <reference osisRef="Ps.51.12">Ps. li. 12</reference>. He likewise taught, (2.) The Hebrew masters not to trample upon their poor servants, knowing, not only that they had been by birth upon a level with them, but that, in a few years, they would be so again. Thus Christian masters must look with respect on believing servants, <reference osisRef="Phlm.1.16">Philem. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen1868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1869" type="x-p"/> 2. This law will be further useful to us, (1.) To illustrate the right God has to the children of believing parents, as such, and the place they have in his church. They are by baptism enrolled among his servants, because they are <hi type="italic">born in his house,</hi> for they are therefore <hi type="italic">born unto him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.20">Ezek. xvi. 20</reference>. David owns himself God's servant, as he was <hi type="italic">the son of his handmaid</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.16">Ps. cxvi. 16</reference>), and therefore entitled to protection, <reference osisRef="Ps.86.16">Ps. lxxxvi. 16</reference>. (2.) To explain the obligation which the great Redeemer laid upon himself to prosecute the work of our salvation, for he says (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.6">Ps. xl. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">My ears hast thou opened,</hi> which seems to allude to this law. He loved his Father, and his captive spouse, and the children that were given him, and would not go out free from his undertaking, but engaged to serve in it for ever, <reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Isa. xlii. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.42.4">4</reference>. Much more reason have we thus to engage ourselves to serve God for ever; we have all the reason in the world to love our Master and his work, and to have our ears bored to his door-posts, as those who desire not to go out free from his service, but to be found more and more free to it, and in it, <reference osisRef="Ps.84.10">Ps. lxxxiv. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen1869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1870" type="x-p"/> Concerning maid-servants, whom their parents, through extreme poverty, had sold, when they were very young, to such as they hoped would marry them when they grew up; if they did not, yet they must not sell them to strangers, but rather study how to make them amends for the disappointment; if they did, they must maintain them handsomely, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.7-Exod.21.11">v. 7-11</reference>. Thus did God provide for the comfort and reputation of the daughters of Israel, and has taught husbands to <hi type="italic">give honour to their wives</hi> (be their extraction ever so mean) as to the <hi type="italic">weaker vessels,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.7">1 Pet. iii. 7</reference>.
entries.90f8f1d8504bbe1e86832e683bb48795eae3e6b1: <div eID="gen1870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1871" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> He that smiteth a man, so that he die, shall be surely put to death. <hi type="super">13</hi> And if a man lie not in wait, but God deliver <hi type="italic">him</hi> into his hand; then I will appoint thee a place whither he shall flee. <hi type="super">14</hi> But if a man come presumptuously upon his neighbour, to slay him with guile; thou shalt take him from mine altar, that he may die. <hi type="super">15</hi> And he that smiteth his father, or his mother, shall be surely put to death. <hi type="super">16</hi> And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death. <hi type="super">17</hi> And he that curseth his father, or his mother, shall surely be put to death. <hi type="super">18</hi> And if men strive together, and one smite another with a stone, or with <hi type="italic">his</hi> fist, and he die not, but keepeth <hi type="italic">his</hi> bed: <hi type="super">19</hi> If he rise again, and walk abroad upon his staff, then shall he that smote <hi type="italic">him</hi> be quit: only he shall pay <hi type="italic">for</hi> the loss of his time, and shall cause <hi type="italic">him</hi> to be thoroughly healed. <hi type="super">20</hi> And if a man smite his servant, or his maid, with a rod, and he die under his hand; he shall be surely punished. <hi type="super">21</hi> Notwithstanding, if he continue a day or two, he shall not be punished: for he <hi type="italic">is</hi> his money. <div eID="gen1871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1872" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A law concerning murder. He had lately said, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not kill;</hi> here he provides, 1. For the punishing of wilful murder (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that smiteth a man,</hi> whether upon a sudden passion or in malice prepense, <hi type="italic">so that he die,</hi> the government must take care that the murderer be <hi type="italic">put to death,</hi> according to that ancient law (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.6">Gen. ix. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed.</hi> God, who by his providence gives and maintains life, thus by his law protects it; so that mercy shown to a wilful murderer is real cruelty to all mankind besides: such a one, God here says, shall be taken even <hi type="italic">from his altar</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.14">v. 14</reference>), to which he might flee for protection; and, if God will not shelter him, let him <hi type="italic">flee to the pit, and let no man stay him.</hi> 2. For the relief of such as killed by accident, <hi type="italic">per infortunium—by misfortune,</hi> or <hi type="italic">chance-medley,</hi> as our law expresses it, when a man, in doing a lawful act, without intent of hurt to any, happens to kill another, or, as it is here described, <hi type="italic">God delivers him into his hand;</hi> for nothing comes to pass by chance; what seems to us purely casual is ordered by the divine Providence, for wise and holy ends secret to us. In this case God provided cities of refuge for the protection of those whose infelicity it was, but not their fault, to occasion the death of another, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.13">v. 13</reference>. With us, who know no avengers of blood but the magistrates, the law itself is a sufficient sanctuary for those whose minds are innocent, though their hands are guilty, and there needs no other. <div eID="gen1872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1873" type="x-p"/> II. Concerning rebellious children. It is here made a capital crime, to be punished with death, for children either, 1. To strike their parents (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.15">v. 15</reference>) so as either to draw blood or to make the place struck black and blue. Or, 2. To curse their parents (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.17">v. 17</reference>), if they profaned any name of God in doing it, as the rabbies say. Note, The undutiful behaviour of children towards their parents is a very great provocation to God our common Father; and, if men do not punish it, he will. Those are perfectly lost to all virtue, and abandoned to all wickedness, that have broken through the bonds of filial reverence and duty to such a degree as in word or action to abuse their own parents. What yoke will those bear that have shaken off this? Let children take heed of entertaining in their minds any such thought or passions towards their parents as savour of undutifulness and contempt; for the righteous God searches the heart. <div eID="gen1873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1874" type="x-p"/> III. Here is a law against man-stealing (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that steals a man</hi> (that is, a person, man, woman, or child), with design to sell him to the Gentiles (for no Israelite would buy him), was adjudged to death by this statute, which is ratified by the apostle (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.10">1 Tim. i. 10</reference>), where <hi type="italic">men-stealers</hi> are reckoned among those wicked ones against whom laws must be made by Christian princes. <div eID="gen1874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1875" type="x-p"/> IV. Care is here taken that satisfaction be made for hurt done to a person, though death do not ensue, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.18-Exod.21.19">v. 18, 19</reference>. He that did the hurt must be accountable for damages, and pay, not only for the cure, but for the loss of time, to which the Jews add that he must likewise give some recompence both for the pain and for the blemish, if there were any. <div eID="gen1875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1876" type="x-p"/> V. Direction is given what should be done if a servant died by his master's correction. This servant must not be an Israelite, but a Gentile slave, as the negroes to our planters; and it is supposed that he smite him with a rod, and not with any thing that was likely to give a mortal wound; yet, if he died under his hand, he should be punished for his cruelty, at the discretion of the judges, upon consideration of circumstances, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.20">v. 20</reference>. But, if he continued a day or two after the correction given, the master was supposed to suffer enough by losing his servant, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.21">v. 21</reference>. Our law makes the death of a servant, by his master's reasonable beating of him, but <hi type="italic">chance-medley.</hi> Yet let all masters take heed of tyrannizing over their servants; the gospel teaches them even to forbear and moderate threatenings (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.9">Eph. vi. 9</reference>), considering with holy Job, <hi type="italic">What shall I do, when God riseth up?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.31.13-Job.31.15">Job xxxi. 13-15</reference>.
entries.cf77fc755dd686749bda43ce0a67b8dbf53d6cca: <div eID="gen1876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1877" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> If men strive, and hurt a woman with child, so that her fruit depart <hi type="italic">from her,</hi> and yet no mischief follow: he shall be surely punished, according as the woman's husband will lay upon him; and he shall pay as the judges <hi type="italic">determine.</hi> <hi type="super">23</hi> And if <hi type="italic">any</hi> mischief follow, then thou shalt give life for life, <hi type="super">24</hi> Eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, <hi type="super">25</hi> Burning for burning, wound for wound, stripe for stripe. <hi type="super">26</hi> And if a man smite the eye of his servant, or the eye of his maid, that it perish; he shall let him go free for his eye's sake. <hi type="super">27</hi> And if he smite out his manservant's tooth, or his maidservant's tooth; he shall let him go free for his tooth's sake. <hi type="super">28</hi> If an ox gore a man or a woman, that they die: then the ox shall be surely stoned, and his flesh shall not be eaten; but the owner of the ox <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> quit. <hi type="super">29</hi> But if the ox were wont to push with his horn in time past, and it hath been testified to his owner, and he hath not kept him in, but that he hath killed a man or a woman; the ox shall be stoned, and his owner also shall be put to death. 30 If there be laid on him a sum of money, then he shall give for the ransom of his life whatsoever is laid upon him. <hi type="super">31</hi> Whether he have gored a son, or have gored a daughter, according to this judgment shall it be done unto him. <hi type="super">32</hi> If the ox shall push a manservant or a maidservant; he shall give unto their master thirty shekels of silver, and the ox shall be stoned. <hi type="super">33</hi> And if a man shall open a pit, or if a man shall dig a pit, and not cover it, and an ox or an ass fall therein; <hi type="super">34</hi> The owner of the pit shall make <hi type="italic">it</hi> good, <hi type="italic">and</hi> give money unto the owner of them; and the dead <hi type="italic">beast</hi> shall be his. <hi type="super">35</hi> And if one man's ox hurt another's, that he die; then they shall sell the live ox, and divide the money of it; and the dead <hi type="italic">ox</hi> also they shall divide. <hi type="super">36</hi> Or if it be known that the ox hath used to push in time past, and his owner hath not kept him in; he shall surely pay ox for ox; and the dead shall be his own. <div eID="gen1877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1878" type="x-p"/> Observe here, <div eID="gen1878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1879" type="x-p"/> I. The particular care which the law took of women with child, that no hurt should be done them which might occasion their mis-carrying. The law of nature obliges us to be very tender in that case, lest the tree and fruit be destroyed together, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.22-Exod.21.23">v. 22, 23</reference>. Women with child, who are thus taken under the special protection of the law of God, if they live in his fear, may still believe themselves under the special protection of the providence of God, and hope that they shall be saved in child-bearing. On this occasion comes in that general law of retaliation which our Saviour refers to, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.38">Matt. v. 38</reference>, <hi type="italic">An eye for an eye.</hi> Now, 1. The execution of this law is not hereby put into the hands of private persons, as if every man might avenge himself, which would introduce universal confusion, and make men like the fishes of the sea. The tradition of the elders seems to have put this corrupt gloss upon it, in opposition to which our Saviour commands us to forgive injuries, and not to meditate revenge, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.39">Matt. v. 39</reference>. 2. God often executes it in the course of his providence, making the punishment, in many cases, to answer to the sin, as <reference osisRef="Judg.1.7">Judg. i. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.1">Isa. xxxiii. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.13">Hab. ii. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.26.52">Matt. xxvi. 52</reference>. 3. Magistrates ought to have an eye to this rule in punishing offenders, and doing right to those that are injured. Consideration must be had of the nature, quality, and degree of the wrong done, that reparation may be made to the party injured, and others deterred from doing the like; either <hi type="italic">an eye</hi> shall go <hi type="italic">for an eye,</hi> or the forfeited eye shall be redeemed by a sum of money. Note, He that does wrong must expect one way or other to receive <hi type="italic">according to the wrong he has done,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.3.25">Col. iii. 25</reference>. God sometimes brings men's violent dealings upon their own heads (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.16">Ps. vii. 16</reference>); and magistrates are in this the ministers of the justice, that they are <hi type="italic">avengers</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.13.4">Rom. xiii. 4</reference>), and they shall not bear the sword in vain. <div eID="gen1879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1880" type="x-p"/> II. The care God took of servants. If their masters maimed them, though it was only striking out a tooth, that should be their discharge, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.26-Exod.21.27">v. 26, 27</reference>. This was intended, 1. To prevent their being abused; masters would be careful not to offer them any violence, lest they should lose their service. 2. To comfort them if they were abused; the loss of a limb should be the gaining of their liberty, which would do something towards balancing both the pain and disgrace they underwent. Nay, <div eID="gen1880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1881" type="x-p"/> III. <hi type="italic">Does God take care for oxen?</hi> Yes, it appears by the following laws in this chapter that he does, <hi type="italic">for our sakes,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.9-1Cor.9.10">1 Cor. ix. 9, 10</reference>. The Israelites are here directed what to do, <div eID="gen1881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1882" type="x-p"/> 1. In case of hurt done by oxen, or any other brute-creature; for the law, doubtless, was designed to extend to all parallel cases. (1.) As an instance of God's care of the life of man (though forfeited a thousand times into the hands of divine justice), and in token of his detestation of the sin of murder. If an ox killed any man, woman, or child, the ox was to be <hi type="italic">stoned</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.28">v. 28</reference>); and, because the greatest honour of the inferior creatures is to be serviceable to man, the criminal is denied that honour: his <hi type="italic">flesh shall not be eaten.</hi> Thus God would keep up in the minds of his people a rooted abhorrence of the sin of murder and every thing that was barbarous. (2.) To make men careful that none of their cattle might do hurt, but that, by all means possible, mischief might be prevented. If the owner of the beast knew that he was mischievous, he must answer for the hurt done, and, according as the circumstances of the case proved him to be more or less accessory, he must either be <hi type="italic">put to death</hi> or ransom his life with a sum of money, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.29-Exod.21.32">v. 29-32</reference>. Some of our ancient books make this felony, by the common law of England, and give this reason, "The owner, by suffering his beast to go at liberty when he knew it to be mischievous, shows that he was very willing that hurt should be done." Note, It is not enough for us not to do mischief ourselves, but we must take care that no mischief be done by those whom it is in our power to restrain, whether man or beast. <div eID="gen1882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1883" type="x-p"/> 2. In case of hurt done to oxen, or other cattle. (1.) If they fall into a pit, and perish there, he that opened the pit must make good the loss, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.33-Exod.21.34">v. 33, 34</reference>. Note, We must take heed not only of doing that which will be hurtful, but of doing that which may be so. It is not enough not to design and devise mischief, but we must contrive to prevent mischief, else we become accessory to our neighbours' damage. Mischief done in malice is the great transgression; but mischief done through negligence, and for want of due care and consideration, is not without fault, but ought to be reflected upon with great regret, according as the degree of the mischief is: especially we must be careful that we do nothing to make ourselves accessory to the sins of others, by laying an occasion of offence in our brother's way, <reference osisRef="Rom.14.13">Rom. xiv. 13</reference>. (2.) If cattle fight, and one kill another, the owners shall equally share in the loss, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.35">v. 35</reference>. Only if the beast that had done the harm was known to the owner to have been mischievous he shall answer for the damage, because he ought either to have killed him or kept him up, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.36">v. 36</reference>. The determinations of these cases carry with them the evidence of their own equity, and give such rules of justice as were then, and are still, in use, for the decision of similar controversies that arise between man and man. But I conjecture that these cases might be specified, rather than others (though some of them seem minute), because they were then cases in fact actually depending before Moses; for in the wilderness where they lay closely encamped, and had their flocks and herds among them, such mischiefs as these last mentioned were likely enough to occur. That which we are taught by these laws is that we should be very careful to do no wrong, either directly or indirectly; and that, if we have done wrong, we must be very willing to make satisfaction, and desirous that nobody may lose by us.  <chapter eID="Exod.21"/> <div eID="gen1883" type="x-p"/>

entries.56d9de0fb8d4822d0683ec8a10086a30bd259d7b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv797"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 21</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Exod.21.1-Exod.21.6">Ex 21:1-6</reference>. Laws for Menservants.</title> <div sID="gen1118" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv797"/><hi type="bold">1. judgments--</hi>rules for regulating the procedure of judges and magistrates in the decision of cases and the trial of criminals. The government of the Israelites being a theocracy, those public authorities were the servants of the Divine Sovereign, and subject to His direction. Most of these laws here noticed were primitive usages, founded on principles of natural equity, and incorporated, with modifications and improvements, in the Mosaic code. <div eID="gen1118" type="x-p"/>
entries.ac84842b89e50cbede93b6a0c4477b0640dca129: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv798"/><div sID="gen1119" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv798"/><hi type="bold">2-6. If thou buy an Hebrew servant--</hi>Every Israelite was free-born; but slavery was permitted under certain restrictions. An Hebrew might be made a slave through poverty, debt, or crime; but at the end of six years he was entitled to freedom, and his wife, if she had voluntarily shared his state of bondage, also obtained release. Should he, however, have married a female slave, she and the children, after the husband's liberation, remained the master's property; and if, through attachment to his family, the Hebrew chose to forfeit his privilege and abide as he was, a formal process was gone through in a public court, and a brand of servitude stamped on his ear (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.6">Psa 40:6</reference>) for life, or at least till the Jubilee (<reference osisRef="Deut.15.17">De 15:17</reference>). <div eID="gen1119" type="x-p"/>
entries.fecbb389ca036ddd514575df90ceb9357c63e908: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv799"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Exod.21.7-Exod.21.36">Ex 21:7-36</reference>. Laws for Maidservants.</title> <div sID="gen1120" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv799"/><hi type="bold">7-11. if a man sell his daughter--</hi>Hebrew girls might be redeemed for a reasonable sum. But in the event of her parents or friends being unable to pay the redemption money, her owner was not at liberty to sell her elsewhere. Should she have been betrothed to him or his son, and either change their minds, a maintenance must be provided for her suitable to her condition as his intended wife, or her freedom instantly granted. <div eID="gen1120" type="x-p"/>
entries.408ad96741545b1f99832ba5f18a214336bb88d0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv800"/><div sID="gen1121" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv800"/><hi type="bold">23-25. eye for eye--</hi>The law which authorized retaliation (a principle acted upon by all primitive people) was a civil one. It was given to regulate the procedure of the public magistrate in determining the amount of compensation in every case of injury, but did not encourage feelings of private revenge. The later Jews, however, mistook it for a moral precept, and were corrected by our Lord (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.38-Matt.5.42">Mt 5:38-42</reference>). <div eID="gen1121" type="x-p"/>
entries.6749980d040235902e33daaac2e71e8ef1dc236a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv801"/><div sID="gen1122" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv801"/><hi type="bold">28-36. If an ox gore a man or a woman, that they die--</hi>For the purpose of sanctifying human blood, and representing all injuries affecting life in a serious light, an animal that occasioned death was to be killed or suffer punishment proportioned to the degree of damage it had caused. Punishments are still inflicted on this principle in Persia and other countries of the East; and among a rude people greater effect is thus produced in inspiring caution, and making them keep noxious animals under restraint, than a penalty imposed on the owners. <div eID="gen1122" type="x-p"/>

entries.a4bceffc72ddc1e7ddcf7f903bc45fd7a4eae64d: <div eID="gen3352" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen3353" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3354" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3354" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3353" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3355" type="x-p"/> Laws concerning servants. They shall serve for only seven years, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.1">Exo 21:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.2">Exo 21:2</reference>. If a servant brought a wife to servitude with him, both should go out free on the seventh year, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.3">Exo 21:3</reference>. If his master had given him a wife, and she bore him children, he might go out free an the seventh year, but his wife and children must remain, as the property of the master, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.4">Exo 21:4</reference>. If, through love to his master, wife, and children, he did not choose to avail himself of the privilege granted by the law, of going out free on the seventh year, his ear was to be bored to the door post with an awl, as an emblem of his being attached to the family for ever, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.5">Exo 21:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.6">Exo 21:6</reference>. Laws concerning maid-servants, betrothed to their masters or to the sons of their masters, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.7-Exo.21.11">Exo 21:7-11</reference>. Laws concerning battery and murder, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.12-Exo.21.15">Exo 21:12-15</reference>. Concerning men-stealing, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.16">Exo 21:16</reference>. Concerning him that curses his parents, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.17">Exo 21:17</reference>. Of strife between man and man, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.18">Exo 21:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.19">Exo 21:19</reference>; between a master and his servants, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.20">Exo 21:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.21">Exo 21:21</reference>. Of injuries done to women in pregnancy, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.22">Exo 21:22</reference>. The Lex Talionis, or law of like, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.23-Exo.21.25">Exo 21:23-25</reference>. Of injuries done to servants, by which they gain the right of freedom, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.26">Exo 21:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.27">Exo 21:27</reference>. Laws concerning the ox which has gored men, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.28-Exo.21.32">Exo 21:28-32</reference>. Of the pit left uncovered, into which a man or a beast has fallen, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.33">Exo 21:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.34">Exo 21:34</reference>. Laws concerning the ox that kills another, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.35">Exo 21:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.36">Exo 21:36</reference>. <div eID="gen3355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3356" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen3356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3357" type="x-p"/> Now these are the judgments - There is so much good sense, feeling, humanity, equity, and justice in the following laws, that they cannot but be admired by every intelligent reader; and they are so very plain as to require very little comment. The laws in this chapter are termed political, those in the succeeding chapter judicial, laws; and are supposed to have been delivered to Moses alone, in consequence of the request of the people, <reference osisRef="Exo.20.19">Exo 20:19</reference>, that God should communicate his will to Moses, and that Moses should, as mediator, convey it to them.
entries.187309a6393e4887f97a639d3813484a438c25ca: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen3357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3358" type="x-p"/> If thou buy a Hebrew servant - Calmet enumerates six different ways in which a Hebrew might lose his liberty: <div eID="gen3358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3359" type="x-p"/> 1. In extreme poverty they might sell their liberty. <reference osisRef="Lev.25.39">Lev 25:39</reference> : If thy brother be waxen poor, and be sold unto thee, etc. <div eID="gen3359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3360" type="x-p"/> 2. A father might sell his children. If a man sell his daughter to be a maidservant; see <reference osisRef="Exo.21.7">Exo 21:7</reference>. <div eID="gen3360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3361" type="x-p"/> 3. Insolvent debtors became the slaves of their creditors. My husband is dead - and the creditor is come to take unto him my two sons to be bondmen, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.1">2Kgs 4:1</reference>. <div eID="gen3361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3362" type="x-p"/> 4. A thief, if he had not money to pay the fine laid on him by the law, was to be sold for his profit whom he had robbed. If he have nothing, then he shall be sold for his theft; <reference osisRef="Exo.22.3">Exo 22:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.22.4">Exo 22:4</reference>. <div eID="gen3362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3363" type="x-p"/> 5. A Hebrew was liable to be taken prisoner in war, and so sold for a slave. <div eID="gen3363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3364" type="x-p"/> 6. A Hebrew slave who had been ransomed from a Gentile by a Hebrew might be sold by him who ransomed him, to one of his own nation. <div eID="gen3364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3365" type="x-p"/> Six years he shall serve - It was an excellent provision in these laws, that no man could finally injure himself by any rash, foolish, or precipitate act. No man could make himself a servant or slave for more than seven years; and if he mortgaged the family inheritance, it must return to the family at the jubilee, which returned every fiftieth year. <div eID="gen3365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3366" type="x-p"/> It is supposed that the term six years is to be understood as referring to the sabbatical years; for let a man come into servitude at whatever part of the interim between two sabbatical years, he could not be detained in bondage beyond a sabbatical year; so that if he fell into bondage the third year after a sabbatical year, he had but three years to serve; if the fifth, but one. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.23.11">Exo 23:11</reference>, etc. Others suppose that this privilege belonged only to the year of jubilee, beyond which no man could be detained in bondage, though he had been sold only one year before.
entries.fd49d2c9500c2b3693427195a12c6358b3541bb2: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen3366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3367" type="x-p"/> If he came in by himself - If he and his wife came in together, they were to go out together: in all respects as he entered, so should he go out. This consideration seems to have induced St. Jerome to translate the passage thus: Cum quali veste intraverat, cum tali exeat. "He shall have the same coat in going out, as he had when he came in," i.e., if he came in with a new one, he shall go out with a new one, which was perfectly just, as the former coat must have been worn out in his master's service, and not his own.
entries.fdedd8a123ddcb4d6fa222ad68a95dd3ace44974: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen3367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3368" type="x-p"/> The wife and her children shall be her master's - It was a law among the Hebrews, that if a Hebrew had children by a Canannitish woman, those children must be considered as Canaanitish only, and might be sold and bought, and serve for ever. The law here refers to such a case only.
entries.3f5d55c6b338f0925d29c729e981bbc922cddcf5: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen3368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3369" type="x-p"/> Shall bring him unto the judges - אל האלהים el haelohim, literally, to God; or, as the Septuagint have it, προς το κριτηριον Θεου, to the judgment of God; who condescended to dwell among his people; who determined all their differences till he had given them laws for all cases, and who, by his omniscience, brought to light the hidden things of dishonesty. See <reference osisRef="Exo.22.8">Exo 22:8</reference>. <div eID="gen3369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3370" type="x-p"/> Bore his ear through with an awl - This was a ceremony sufficiently significant, as it implied, <div eID="gen3370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3371" type="x-p"/> 1. That he was closely attached to that house and family. <div eID="gen3371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3372" type="x-p"/> 2. That he was bound to hear all his master's orders, and to obey them punctually. Boring of the ear was an ancient custom in the east. It is referred to by Juvenal: - <div eID="gen3372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3373" type="x-p"/> Prior, inquit, ego adsum. <div eID="gen3373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3374" type="x-p"/> Cur timeam, dubitemve locum defendere? Quamvis <div eID="gen3374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3375" type="x-p"/> Natus ad Euphraten, Molles quod in Aure Fenestrae <div eID="gen3375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3376" type="x-p"/> Arguerint, licet ipse negem. <div eID="gen3376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3377" type="x-p"/> Sat. i. 102. "First come, first served, he cries; and I, in spite <div eID="gen3377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3378" type="x-p"/> Of your great lordships, will maintain my right: <div eID="gen3378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3379" type="x-p"/> Though born a slave, though my torn Ears are Bored, 'Tis not the birth, 'tis money makes the lord." <div eID="gen3379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3380" type="x-p"/> Dryden. <div eID="gen3380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3381" type="x-p"/> Calmet quotes a saying from Petronius as attesting the same thing; and one from Cicero, in which he rallies a Libyan who pretended he did not hear him: "It is not," said he, "because your ears are not sufficiently bored;" alluding to his having been a slave.
entries.f6def405d08686e66388d8b751013047d07543ed: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen3381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3382" type="x-p"/> If a man sell his daughter - This the Jews allowed no man to do but in extreme distress - when he had no goods, either movable or immovable left, even to the clothes on his back; and he had this permission only while she was unmarriageable. It may appear at first view strange that such a law should have been given; but let it be remembered, that this servitude could extend, at the utmost, only to six years; and that it was nearly the same as in some cases of apprenticeship among us, where the parents bind the child for seven years, and have from the master so much per week during that period.
entries.5191e8d86aa09a2657c27491391261268c0ba656: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen3382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3383" type="x-p"/> Betrothed her unto his son, he shall deal with her - He shall give her the same dowry he would give to one of his own daughters. From these laws we learn, that if a man's son married his servant, by his father's consent, the father was obliged to treat her in every respect as a daughter; and if the son married another woman, as it appears he might do, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.10">Exo 21:10</reference>, he was obliged to make no abatement in the privileges of the first wife, either in her food, raiment, or duty of marriage. The word ענתה onathah, here, is the same with St. Paul's οφειλομενην ευνοιαν, the marriage debt, and with the ὁμιλιαν of the Septuagint, which signifies the cohabitation of man and wife.
entries.f07f7da8a8456fed4bd8c1cd5a04101b42449a73: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen3383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3384" type="x-p"/> These three - <div eID="gen3384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3385" type="x-p"/> 1. Her food, שארה sheerah, her flesh, for she must not, like a common slave, be fed merely on vegetables. <div eID="gen3385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3386" type="x-p"/> 2. Her raiment - her private wardrobe, with all occasional necessary additions. And, <div eID="gen3386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3387" type="x-p"/> 3. The marriage debt - a due proportion of the husband's time and company.
entries.42450f4b5a830b54cf5672dccf567d58c880e349: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen3387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3388" type="x-p"/> I will appoint thee a place whither he shall flee - From the earliest times the nearest akin had a right to revenge the murder of his relation, and as this right was universally acknowledged, no law was ever made on the subject; but as this might be abused, and a person who had killed another accidentally, having had no previous malice against him, might be put to death by the avenger of blood, as the nearest kinsman was termed, therefore God provided the cities of refuge to which the accidental manslayer might flee till the affair was inquired into, and settled by the civil magistrate.
entries.197eac4a6840acf4b62271c3648af96f1a64468f: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen3388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3389" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt take him from mine altar - Before the cities of refuge were assigned, the altar of God was the common asylum.
entries.8f54b60bc7c2aad223faca06206981721e2aba0b: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen3389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3390" type="x-p"/> That smiteth his father, or his mother - As such a case argued peculiar depravity, therefore no mercy was to be shown to the culprit.
entries.939663f7ece1b7c00fd7a43e68b256f9b244c2ff: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen3390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3391" type="x-p"/> He that stealeth a man - By this law every man-stealer, and every receiver of the stolen person, should lose his life; no matter whether the latter stole the man himself, or gave money to a slave captain or negro-dealer to steal him for him.
entries.ada51af2f4824676021bb4d49243fdd51af2f20e: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen3391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3392" type="x-p"/> Shall pay for the loss of his time, and shall cause him to be thoroughly healed - This was a wise and excellent institution, and most courts of justice still regulate their decisions on such cases by this Mosaic precept.
entries.76e49545db846f7a2932e013e13b61c078021fdb: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen3392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3393" type="x-p"/> If the slave who had been beaten by his master died under his hand, the master was punished with death - see <reference osisRef="Gen.9.5">Gen 9:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.9.6">Gen 9:6</reference>. But if he survived the beating a day or two the master was not punished, because it might be presumed that the man died through some other cause. And all penal laws should be construed as favourably as possible to the accused.
entries.c691d105126e26d47d2a5b29ef48f93483e90436: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen3393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3394" type="x-p"/> And hurt a woman with child - As a posterity among the Jews was among the peculiar promises of their covenant, and as every man had some reason to think that the Messiah should spring from his family, therefore any injury done to a woman with child, by which the fruit of her womb might be destroyed, was considered a very heavy offense; and as the crime was committed principally against the husband, the degree of punishment was left to his discretion. But if mischief followed, that is, if the child had been fully formed, and was killed by this means, or the woman lost her life in consequence, then the punishment was as in other cases of murder - the person was put to death; <reference osisRef="Exo.21.23">Exo 21:23</reference>.
entries.87a3eb96202054ff9e5453ff0d6b76a7db5ec400: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen3394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3395" type="x-p"/> Eye for eye - This is the earliest account we have of the lex talionis, or law of like for like, which afterwards prevailed among the Greeks and Romans. Among the latter, it constituted a part of the twelve tables, so famous in antiquity; but the punishment was afterwards changed to a pecuniary fine, to be levied at the discretion of the praetor. It prevails less or more in most civilized countries, and is fully acted upon in the canon law, in reference to all calumniators: Calumniator, si in accusatione defecerit, talionem recipiat. "If the calumniator fall in the proof of his accusation, let him suffer the same punishment which he wished to have inflicted upon the man whom he falsely accused." Nothing, however, of this kind was left to private revenge; the magistrate awarded the punishment when the fact was proved, otherwise the lex talionis would have utterly destroyed the peace of society, and have sown the seeds of hatred, revenge, and all uncharitableness.
entries.b142b8fbef7f87c337f332e8142d77a7adcbef13: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen3395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3396" type="x-p"/> If a man smite the eye, etc. - See the following verse.
entries.ac1416257fa1546a6365e46c85806cd0223b6f6e: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen3396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3397" type="x-p"/> If he smite out his - tooth - It was a noble law that obliged the unmerciful slaveholder to set the slave at liberty whose eye or tooth he had knocked out. If this did not teach them humanity, it taught them caution, as one rash blow might have deprived them of all right to the future services of the slave; and thus self-interest obliged them to be cautious and circumspect.
entries.46596c95500d68e93c770c5b30273c6c1e3ad47f: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen3397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3398" type="x-p"/> If an ox gore a man - It is more likely that a bull is here intended, as the word signifies both, see <reference osisRef="Exo.22.1">Exo 22:1</reference>; and the Septuagint translate the שור shor of the original by ταυρος, a bull. Mischief of this kind was provided against by most nations. It appears that the Romans twisted hay about the horns of their dangerous cattle, that people seeing it might shun them; hence that saying of Horace. Sat., lib. i., sat. 4, ver. 34: Faenum habet in cornu, longe fuge. "He has hay on his horns; fly for life!" The laws of the twelve tables ordered, That the owner of the beast should pay for what damages he committed, or deliver him to the person injured. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.22.1">Exo 22:1</reference>. <div eID="gen3398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3399" type="x-p"/> His flesh shall not be eaten - This served to keep up a due detestation of murder, whether committed by man or beast; and at the same time punished the man as far as possible, by the total loss of the beast.
entries.609e9d01edd7eff301d7ee9072da968ce1dd46ea: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen3399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3400" type="x-p"/> If there be laid on him a sum of money - the ransom of his life - So it appears that, though by the law he forfeited his life, yet this might be commuted for a pecuniary mulct, at which the life of the deceased might be valued by the magistrates.
entries.fdcfff2cfc2d668e8f82991ea7c06dfbbf6905f4: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen3400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3401" type="x-p"/> Thirty shekels - Each worth about three shillings English; see <reference osisRef="Gen.20.16">Gen 20:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.23.15">Gen 23:15</reference>. So, counting the shekel at its utmost value, the life of a slave was valued at four pounds ten shillings. And at this price these same vile people valued the life of our blessed Lord; see <reference osisRef="Zac.11.12">Zac 11:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zac.11.13">Zac 11:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mat.26.15">Mat 26:15</reference>. And in return, the justice of God has ordered it so, that they have been sold for slaves into every country of the universe. And yet, strange to tell, they see not the hand of God in so visible a retribution!
entries.b0241d353de9f1b4d11b78063993d619e03ecae9: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen3401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3402" type="x-p"/> And if a man shall open a pit, or - dig a pit - That is, if a man shall open a well or cistern that had been before closed up, or dig a new one; for these two cases are plainly intimated: and if he did this in some public place where there was danger that men or cattle might fall into it; for a man might do as he pleased in his own grounds, as those were his private right. In the above case, if he had neglected to cover the pit, and his neighbor's ox or ass was killed by falling into it, he was to pay its value in money. <reference osisRef="Exo.21.33">Exo 21:33</reference> and <reference osisRef="Exo.21.34">Exo 21:34</reference> seem to be out of their places. They probably should conclude the chapters, as, where they are, they interrupt the statutes concerning the goring ox, which begin at <reference osisRef="Exo.21.28">Exo 21:28</reference>. <div eID="gen3402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3403" type="x-p"/> These different regulations are as remarkable for their justice and prudence as for their humanity. Their great tendency is to show the valuableness of human life, and the necessity of having peace and good understanding in every neighborhood; and they possess that quality which should be the object of all good and wholesome laws - the prevention of crimes. Most criminal codes of jurisprudence seem more intent on the punishment of crimes than on preventing the commission of them. The law of God always teaches and warns, that his creatures may not fall into condemnation; for judgment is his strange work, i.e., one reluctantly and seldom executed, as this text is frequently understood.  <chapter eID="Exod.21"/> <div eID="gen3403" type="x-p"/>

entries.7cd301a417cdeee8af5168243bcd3cb92eb10bb8: The <hi type="italic">mishpatim</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.1">Exo 21:1</reference>) are not the “laws, which were to be in force and serve as rules of action,” as <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> affirms, but the <hi type="italic">rights</hi>, by which the national life was formed into a civil commonwealth and the political order secured. These rights had reference first of all to the relation in which the individuals stood one towards another. The <hi type="italic">personal rights</hi> of dependants are placed at the head (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.2-Exod.21.11">Exo 21:2-11</reference>); and first those of slaves (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.2-Exod.21.6">Exo 21:2-6</reference>), which are still more minutely explained in <reference osisRef="Deut.15.12-Deut.15.18">Deu 15:12-18</reference>, where the observance of them is urged upon the hearts of the people on subjective grounds.
entries.4881d36c278400d7cbdd1aff876d6f05dd54dae8: <reference osisRef="Exod.21.2">Exo 21:2</reference> <div eID="gen912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen913" type="x-p"/> The Hebrew servant was to obtain his freedom without paying compensation, after six years of service. According to <reference osisRef="Deut.15.12">Deu 15:12</reference>, this rule applied to the Hebrew maid-servant as well. The predicate עברי limits the rule to Israelitish servants, in distinction from slaves of foreign extraction, to whom this law did not apply (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.15.12">Deu 15:12</reference>, “thy brother”).<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Saalschütz</hi> is quite wrong in his supposition, that עברי relates not to Israelites, but to relations of the Israelites who had come over to them from their original native land. (See my <hi type="italic">Archδologie</hi>, §112, Note 2.)</note> <div eID="gen913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen914" type="x-p"/> An Israelite might buy his own countryman, either when he was sold by a court of justice on account of theft (<reference osisRef="Exod.22.1">Exo 22:1</reference>), or when he was poor and sold himself (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.39">Lev 25:39</reference>). The emancipation in the seventh year of service was intimately connected with the sabbatical year, though we are not to understand it as taking place in that particular year. “He shall go out free,” sc., from his master’s house, i.e., be set at liberty. חנּם: without compensation. In Deuteronomy the master is also commanded not to let him go out empty, but to load him (חעניק to put upon his neck) from his flock, his threshing-floor, and his wine-press (i.e., with corn and wine); that is to say, to give him as much as he could carry away with him. The motive for this command is drawn from their recollection of their own deliverance by Jehovah from the bondage of Egypt. And in <reference osisRef="Exod.21.18">Exo 21:18</reference> an additional reason is supplied, to incline the heart of the master to this emancipation, viz., that “he has served thee for six years the double of a labourer’s wages,” - that is to say, “he has served and worked so much, that it would have cost twice as much, if it had been necessary to hire a labourer in his place” (<hi type="italic">Schultz</hi>), - and “Jehovah thy God hath blessed thee in all that thou doest,” sc., through his service.
entries.9c12cb9c2ec2239d3549ce1dc2745263d46ee337: <reference osisRef="Exod.21.3-Exod.21.6">Exo 21:3-6</reference> <div eID="gen914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen915" type="x-p"/> There were three different circumstances possible, under which emancipation might take place. The servant might have been unmarried and continued so (בּגפּו: with his body, i.e., alone, single): in that case, of course, there was no one else to set at liberty. Or he might have brought a wife with him; and in that case his wife was to be set at liberty as well. Or his master might have given him a wife in his bondage, and she might have borne him children: in that case the wife and children were to continue the property of the master. This may appear oppressive, but it was an equitable consequence of the possession of property in slaves at all. At the same time, in order to modify the harshness of such a separation of husband and wife, the option was given to the servant to remain in his master’s service, provided he was willing to renounce his liberty for ever (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.5">Exo 21:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.6">Exo 21:6</reference>). This would very likely be the case as a general rule; for there were various legal arrangements, which are mentioned in other places, by which the lot of Hebrew slaves was greatly softened and placed almost on an equality with that of hired labourers (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.23.12">Exo 23:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.25.6">Lev 25:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.25.39">Lev 25:39</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.25.43">Lev 25:43</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.25.53">Lev 25:53</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.12.18">Deu 12:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.16.11">Deu 16:11</reference>). In this case the master was to take his servant האלהים אל, lit., <hi type="italic">to God,</hi> i.e., according to the correct rendering of the lxx, πρὸς τὸ κριτήριον, to the place where judgment was given in the name of God (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.17">Deu 1:17</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.22.7-Exod.22.8">Exo 22:7-8</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Deut.19.17">Deu 19:17</reference>), in order that he might make a declaration there that he gave up his liberty. His ear was then to be bored with an awl against the door or lintel of the house, and by this sign, which was customary in many of the nations of antiquity, to be fastened as it were to the house for ever. That this was the meaning of the piercing of the ear against the door of the house, is evident from the unusual expression in <reference osisRef="Deut.15.17">Deu 15:17</reference>, “and put (the awl) into his ear and into the door, that he may be thy servant for ever,” where the ear and the door are co-ordinates. “<hi type="italic">For ever,</hi>” i.e., as long as he lives. <hi type="italic">Josephus</hi> and the Rabbins would restrict the service to the time ending with the year of jubilee, but without sufficient reason, and contrary to the usage of the language, as לעלם is used in <reference osisRef="Lev.25.46">Lev 25:46</reference> to denote service which did not terminate with the year of jubilee. (See the remarks on <reference osisRef="Lev.25.10">Lev 25:10</reference>; also my <hi type="italic">Archäologie</hi>.)
entries.f53444753d095c706f2686157b491eea7cfafd3b: <reference osisRef="Exod.21.7-Exod.21.11">Exo 21:7-11</reference> <div eID="gen915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen916" type="x-p"/> The daughter of an Israelite, who had been sold by her father as a maid-servant (לאמה), i.e., as the sequel shows, as a housekeeper and concubine, stood in a different relation to her master’s house. She was not to go out like the men-servants, i.e., not to be sent away as free at the end of six years of service; but the three following regulations, which are introduced by אם (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.8">Exo 21:8</reference>), ואם (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.9">Exo 21:9</reference>), and ואם (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.11">Exo 21:11</reference>), were to be observed with regard to her. In the <hi type="italic">first</hi> place (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.8">Exo 21:8</reference>), “<hi type="italic">if she please not her master, who hath betrothed her to himself, then shall he let her be redeemed.</hi>” The לא before יעדהּ is one of the fifteen cases in which לא has been marked in the Masoretic text as standing for לו; and it cannot possibly signify <hi type="italic">not</hi> in the passage before us. For if it were to be taken as a negative, “that he do not appoint her,” sc., as a concubine for himself, the pronoun לו would certainly not be omitted. הפדּהּ (for הפדּהּ, see <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> §53, Note 6), to let her be redeemed, i.e., to allow another Israelite to buy her as a concubine; for there can hardly have been any thought of redemption on the part of the father, as it would no doubt be poverty alone that caused him to sell his daughter (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.39">Lev 25:39</reference>). But “<hi type="italic">to sell her unto a strange nation</hi> (i.e., to any one but a Hebrew), <hi type="italic">he shall have no power, if he acts unfaithfully towards her,</hi>” i.e., if he do not grant her the promised marriage. In the second place (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.9">Exo 21:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.10">Exo 21:10</reference>), “<hi type="italic">if he appoint her as his son’s wife, he shall act towards her according to the rights of daughters,</hi>” i.e., treat her as a daughter; “and if he take him (the son) another (wife), - whether because the son was no longer satisfied, or because the father gave the son another wife in addition to her - “<hi type="italic">her food</hi> (שׁאר flesh as the chief article of food, instead of לחם, bread, because the lawgiver had persons of property in his mind, who were in a position to keep concubines), <hi type="italic">her raiment, and her duty of marriage he shall not diminish,</hi>” i.e., the claims which she had as a daughter for support, and as his son’s wife for conjugal rights, were not to be neglected; he was not to allow his son, therefore, to put her away or treat her badly. With this explanation the difficulties connected with every other are avoided. For instance, if we refer the words of <reference osisRef="Exod.21.9">Exo 21:9</reference> to the son, and understand them as meaning, “if the son should take another wife,” we introduce a change of subject without anything to indicate it. If, on the other hand, we regard them as meaning, “if the father (the purchaser) should take to himself another wife,” this ought to have come before Exo 21:9. In the <hi type="italic">third</hi> place (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.11">Exo 21:11</reference>), “<hi type="italic">if he do not</hi> (do not grant) <hi type="italic">these three unto her, she shall go out for nothing, without money</hi>.” “These three” are food, clothing, and conjugal rights, which are mentioned just before; not “<hi type="italic">si eam non desponderit sibi nec filio, nec redimi sit passus</hi>” (<hi type="italic">Rabbins</hi> and others), nor “if he did not give her to his son as a concubine, but diminished her,” as <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> explains it. <div eID="gen916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen917" type="x-p"/> Still higher than personal liberty, however, is life itself, the right of existence and personality; and the infliction of injury upon this was not only prohibited, but to be followed by punishment corresponding to the crime. The principle of retribution, <hi type="italic">jus talionis</hi>, which is the only one that embodies the idea of justice, lies at the foundation of these threats.
entries.e075fef2327dea27dcaf7618949e596dc8961da9: <reference osisRef="Exod.21.12-Exod.21.13">Exo 21:12-13</reference> <div eID="gen917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen918" type="x-p"/> A <hi type="italic">death-blow</hi> was to be punished with death (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.9.6">Gen 9:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.24.17">Lev 24:17</reference>). “<hi type="italic">He that smiteth a man and</hi> (so that) <hi type="italic">he die</hi> (whether on the spot or directly afterwards did not matter), <hi type="italic">he shall be put to death</hi>.” This general rule is still further defined by a distinction being drawn between accidental and intentional killing. “<hi type="italic">But whoever has not lain in wait</hi> (for another’s life), <hi type="italic">and God has caused it to come to his hand</hi>” (to kill the other); i.e., not only if he did not intend to kill him, but did not even cherish the intention of smiting him, or of doing him harm from hatred and enmity (Num 35:16-23; <reference osisRef="Deut.19.4-Deut.19.5">Deu 19:4-5</reference>), and therefore did so quite unawares, according to a dispensation of God, which is generally called an accident because it is above our comprehension. For such a man God would appoint places of refuge, where he should be protected against the avenger of blood. (On this point, see Num 35:9.).
entries.389a6044cb3063a3e3c009275f682593da9c6b41: <reference osisRef="Exod.21.14-Exod.21.17">Exo 21:14-17</reference> <div eID="gen918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen919" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">But he who acts presumptuously against his neighbour, to slay him with guile, thou shalt take him from Mine altar that he may die</hi>.” These words are not to be understood as meaning, that only intentional and treacherous killing was to be punished with death; but, without restricting the general rule in <reference osisRef="Exod.21.12">Exo 21:12</reference>, they are to be interpreted from their antithesis to <reference osisRef="Exod.21.13">Exo 21:13</reference>, as signifying that even the altar of Jehovah was not to protect a man who had committed intentional murder, and carried out his purpose with treachery. (More on this point at Num 35:16.) By this regulation, the idea, which was common to the Hebrews and many other nations, that the altar as God’s abode afforded protection to any life that was in danger from men, was brought back to the true measure of its validity, and the place of expiation for sins of weakness (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.4.2">Lev 4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.5.15">Lev 5:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.5.18">Lev 5:18</reference>; Num 15:27-31) was prevented from being abused by being made a place of refuge for criminals who were deserving of death. Maltreatment of a father and mother through striking (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.15">Exo 21:15</reference>), man-stealing (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.16">Exo 21:16</reference>), and cursing parents (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.17">Exo 21:17</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.20.9">Lev 20:9</reference>), were all to be placed on a par with murder, and punished in the same way. By the “<hi type="italic">smiting</hi>” (הכּה) <hi type="italic">of parents</hi> we are not to understand smiting to death, for in that case ומת would be added as in <reference osisRef="Exod.21.12">Exo 21:12</reference>, but any kind of maltreatment. The murder of parents is not mentioned at all, as not likely to occur and hardly conceivable. The <hi type="italic">cursing</hi> (קלּל as in <reference osisRef="Gen.12.3">Gen 12:3</reference>) <hi type="italic">of parents </hi>is placed on a par with smiting, because it proceeds from the same disposition; and both were to be punished with death, because the majesty of God was violated in the persons of the parents (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.20.12">Exo 20:12</reference>). <hi type="italic">Man-stealing</hi> was also no less a crime, being a sin against the <hi type="italic">dignity</hi> of man, and a violation of the image of God. For אישׁ “a man,” we find in <reference osisRef="Deut.24.7">Deu 24:7</reference>, נפשׁ “a soul,” by which both man and woman are intended, and the still more definite limitation, “of his brethren of the children of Israel.” The crime remained the same whether he had sold him (the stolen man), or whether he was still found in his hand. (For ו - ו as a sign of an alternative in the linking together of short sentences, see <reference osisRef="Prov.29.9">Pro 29:9</reference>, and Ewald, §361.) This is the rendering adopted by most of the earlier translators, and we get no intelligent sense if we divide the clauses thus: “and sell him so that he is found in his hand.” <div eID="gen919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen920" type="x-p"/> Fatal blows and the crimes placed on a par with them are now followed in simple order by the laws relating to <hi type="italic">bodily injuries</hi>.
entries.a8c0d7fe0c4425af26d3f62a5e36c55bec004cba: <reference osisRef="Exod.21.18-Exod.21.19">Exo 21:18-19</reference> <div eID="gen920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen921" type="x-p"/> If in the course of a quarrel one man should hit another with a stone or with his fist, so that, although he did not die, he “<hi type="italic">lay upon his bed,</hi>” i.e., became bedridden; if the person struck should get up again and walk out with his staff, the other would be innocent, he should “<hi type="italic">only give him his sitting and have him cured,</hi>” i.e., compensate him for his loss of time and the cost of recovery. This certainly implies, on the one hand, that if the man died upon his bed, the injury was to be punished with death, according to <reference osisRef="Exod.21.12">Exo 21:12</reference>; and on the other hand, that if he died after getting up and going out, no further punishment was to be inflicted for the injury done.
entries.a3a35d028f3e683ef695f51b6e3293002133a1a6: <reference osisRef="Exod.21.20-Exod.21.21">Exo 21:20-21</reference> <div eID="gen921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen922" type="x-p"/> The case was different with regard to a slave. The master had always the right to punish or “chasten” him with a stick (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.13">Pro 10:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.13.24">Pro 13:24</reference>); this right was involved in the paternal authority of the master over the servants in his possession. The law was therefore confined to the abuse of this authority in outbursts of passion, in which case, “<hi type="italic">if the servant or the maid should die under his hand</hi> (i.e., under his blows), <hi type="italic">he was to be punished</hi>” (ינּקם נקם: “vengeance shall surely be taken”). But in what the נקם was to consist is not explained; certainly not in slaying by the sword, as the Jewish commentators maintain. The lawgiver would have expressed this by יוּמת מות. No doubt it was left to the authorities to determine this according to the circumstances. The law in <reference osisRef="Exod.21.12">Exo 21:12</reference> could hardly be applied to a case of this description, although it was afterwards extended to foreigners as well as natives (<reference osisRef="Lev.24.21-Lev.24.22">Lev 24:21-22</reference>), for the simple reason, that it is hardly conceivable that a master would intentionally kill his slave, who was his possession and money. How far the lawgiver was from presupposing any such intention here, is evident from the law which follows in <reference osisRef="Exod.21.21">Exo 21:21</reference>, “Notwithstanding, if he continue a day or two (i.e., remain alive), it shall not be avenged, for he is his money.” By the continuance of his life, if only for a day or two, it would become perfectly evident that the master did not wish to kill his servant; and if nevertheless he died after this, the loss of the slave was punishment enough for the master. There is no ground whatever for restricting this regulation, as the Rabbins do, to slaves who were not of Hebrew extraction.
entries.714b56e1bceae249bbc4314e047593760a523221: <reference osisRef="Exod.21.22-Exod.21.25">Exo 21:22-25</reference> <div eID="gen922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen923" type="x-p"/> If men strove and thrust against a woman with child, who had come near or between them for the purpose of making peace, so that her children come out (come into the world), and no injury was done either to the woman or the child that was born,<note placement="foot">The words ילדיה ויצאוּ are rendered by the lxx καὶ ἐξέλθη τὸ παιδίον αὐτῆς μὴ ἐξεικονισμένον and the corresponding clause יהיה אסון ואם by ἐὰν δὲ ἐξεικονισμένον ᾖ; consequently the translators have understood the words as meaning that the fruit, the premature birth of which was caused by the blow, if not yet developed into a human form, was not to be regarded as in any sense a human being, so that the giver of the blow was only required to pay a pecuniary compensation, - as <hi type="italic">Philo</hi> expresses it, “on account of the injury done to the woman, and because he prevented nature, which forms and shapes a man into the most beautiful being, from bringing him forth alive.” But the arbitrary character of this explanation is apparent at once; for ילד only denotes a child, as a fully developed human being, and not the fruit of the womb before it has assumed a human form. In a manner no less arbitrary אסון has been rendered by <hi type="italic">Onkelos</hi> and the <hi type="italic">Rabbins</hi> מותא, death, and the clause is made to refer to the death of the mother alone, in opposition to the penal sentence in <reference osisRef="Exod.21.23">Exo 21:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.24">Exo 21:24</reference>, which not only demands life for life, but eye for eye, etc., and therefore presupposes not death alone, but injury done to particular members. The omission of להּ, also, apparently renders it impracticable to refer the words to injury done to the woman alone.</note> a pecuniary compensation was to be paid, such as the husband of the woman laid upon him, and he was to give it בּפללים by (by an appeal to) arbitrators. A fine is imposed, because even if no injury had been done to the woman and the fruit of her womb, such a blow might have endangered life. (For יצא roF(  to go out of the womb, see <reference osisRef="Gen.25.25">Gen 25:25</reference>-26.) The plural ילדיה is employed for the purpose of speaking indefinitely, because there might possibly be more than one child in the womb. “<hi type="italic">But if injury occur</hi> (to the mother or the child), <hi type="italic">thou shalt give soul for soul, eye for eye,...wound for wound:</hi>” thus perfect retribution was to be made.
entries.39d4b8ba79b67df90f06073f339c0fb3e52132ea: <reference osisRef="Exod.21.26-Exod.21.27">Exo 21:26-27</reference> <div eID="gen923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen924" type="x-p"/> But the <hi type="italic">lex talionis</hi> applied to the free Israelite only, not to slaves. In the case of the latter, if the master struck out an eye and destroyed it, i.e., blinded him with the blow, or struck out a tooth, he was to let him go free, as a compensation for the loss of the member. Eye and tooth are individual examples selected to denote all the members, from the most important and indispensable down to the very least.
entries.acf623e55b77f5f3746951de848194022e952529: <reference osisRef="Exod.21.28-Exod.21.30">Exo 21:28-30</reference> <div eID="gen924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen925" type="x-p"/> The life of man is also protected against injury from cattle (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.9.5">Gen 9:5</reference>). “<hi type="italic">If an ox gore a man or a woman, that they die, the ox shall be stoned, and its flesh shall not be eaten;</hi>” because, as the stoning already shows, it was laden with the guilt of murder, and therefore had become unclean (cf. Num 35:33). The master or owner of the ox was innocent, sc., if his ox had not bee known to do so before. But if this were the case, “<hi type="italic">if his master have been warned</hi> (בּבעליו הוּעד, lit., testimony laid against its master), <hi type="italic">and notwithstanding this he have not kept it in,</hi>” then the master was to be put to death, because through his carelessness in keeping the ox he had caused the death, and therefore shared the guilt. As this guilt, however, had not been incurred through an intentional crime, but had arisen simply from carelessness, he was allowed to redeem his forfeited life by the payment of expiation money (כּפר, lit., covering, expiation, cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.30.12">Exo 30:12</reference>), “<hi type="italic">according to all that was laid upon him,</hi>” sc., by the judge.
entries.c8ee2a0744abc988998eb2c7b2dcb8ae91146ccc: <reference osisRef="Exod.21.31-Exod.21.32">Exo 21:31-32</reference> <div eID="gen925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen926" type="x-p"/> The death of a son or a daughter through the goring of an ox was also to be treated in the same way; but that of a slave (man-servant or maid-servant) was to be compensated by the payment of thirty shekels of silver (i.e., probably the ordinary price for the redemption of a slave, as the redemption price of a free Israelite was fifty shekels, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.3">Lev 27:3</reference>) on the part of the owner of the ox; but the ox was to be killed in this case also. There are other ancient nations in whose law books we find laws relating to the punishment of animals for killing or wounding a man, but not one of them had a law which made the owner of the animal responsible as well, for they none of them looked upon human life in its likeness of God.
entries.95ff75045a4ca0e518faf0d3dcf033618c556f98: <reference osisRef="Exod.21.33-Exod.21.36">Exo 21:33-36</reference> <div eID="gen926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen927" type="x-p"/> Passing from life to <hi type="italic">property</hi>, in connection with the foregoing, the life of the animal, the most important possession of the Israelites, is first of all secured against destruction through carelessness. If any one opened or dug a pit or cistern, and did not close it up again, and another man’s ox or ass (mentioned, for the sake of example, as the most important animals among the live stock of the Israelites) fell in and was killed, the owner of the pit was to pay its full value, and the dead animal to belong to him. If an ox that was not known to be vicious gored another man’s ox to death, the vicious animal was to be sold, and its money (what it fetched) to be divided; the dead animal was also to be divided, so that both parties bore an equal amount of damage. If, on the other hand, the ox had been known to be vicious before, and had not been kept in, carefully secured, by its possessor, he was to compensate the owner of the one that had been killed with the full value of an ox, but to receive the dead one instead.  <chapter eID="Exod.21"/> <div eID="gen927" type="x-p"/>

entries.976fc1f0252e93ae23560dcf56c6b913f1488336:
1. Now these are the judgments. Both passages contain the same appointment, viz., that as to the Hebrews slavery must end at the seventh year; for God would have the children of Abraham, although obliged to sell themselves, to differ from heathen and ordinary slaves. Their enfranchisement is, therefore, enjoined, but with an exception, which Moses expresses in the first passage but omits in the latter, i e., that if the slave had married a bond-woman, and had begotten children, they should remain with the master, and that he should alone be free. Whence it appears how hard was the condition of slaves, since it could not be mitigated without an unnatural exception (sine prodigio;) for nothing could be more opposed to nature than that a husband, forsaking his wife and children, should remove himself elsewhere. But the tie of slavery could only be loosed by divorce, that is to say, by this impious violation of marriage. There was then gross barbarity in this severance, whereby a man was disunited from half of himself and his own bowels.
